what_its_for: Sacituzumab govitecan is a targeted cancer medicine used to treat certain types of breast cancer (including triple-negative breast cancer and HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer) and bladder cancer (urothelial cancer) in adults who have already tried other treatments. It works by finding cancer cells and delivering a powerful chemotherapy drug directly to them to help slow or stop cancer growth.
how_to_take: This medicine is given to you by a healthcare provider as an intravenous (IV) infusion — meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or IV line. You will NOT take this at home as a pill or injection. You will visit your doctor's office, clinic, or infusion center to receive each dose. Your first infusion will take about 3 hours. If you tolerate it well, later infusions may take about 1 to 2 hours. Before each infusion, your care team will give you medicines to help prevent nausea, vomiting, and allergic reactions.
dosing: The usual dose is 10 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given once a week on Days 1 and 8 of a 21-day cycle (3-week cycle). This means you receive an infusion one week, skip the next week, then start again. Your doctor may lower your dose or delay treatment if you experience serious side effects. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider, missing a dose means your scheduled infusion appointment was not completed. If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do NOT try to catch up on your own. Your doctor will decide the best time to give your next dose safely.
storage: You do not store this medicine at home — it is prepared and stored by your healthcare team or pharmacy. If you have any questions about how it is handled, ask your care team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine can weaken your immune system and make it harder to fight illness. Avoid activities that could cause cuts or bleeding since this medicine can lower your platelet count. Do NOT receive live vaccines (such as flu nasal spray, shingles, or MMR vaccines) during treatment without asking your doctor first. Talk to your doctor before taking any new medications, supplements, or herbal products. Avoid becoming pregnant during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose — this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Men should avoid fathering a child during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 1 month after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: severe diarrhea (more than 4 loose stools per day), severe nausea or vomiting that you cannot control, fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher especially with chills (this could be a sign of serious infection called febrile neutropenia), unusual bruising or bleeding, shortness of breath or chest pain, signs of an allergic reaction during or after your infusion such as rash, hives, flushing, dizziness, or trouble breathing, mouth sores that make it hard to eat or drink, extreme fatigue or weakness, yellowing of your skin or eyes (possible liver problem), or any other symptom that worries you. Do not wait — early action can prevent serious harm.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away to target cancer cells, but you may not see or feel results immediately. Your doctor will monitor how well the treatment is working through regular scans and blood tests, usually after a few treatment cycles (every few weeks). Some patients notice improvements within a few months. Keep all follow-up appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: This medicine can seriously harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for 6 months after the last dose. Men with partners who can become pregnant should use birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for 1 month after the last dose. Older Adults (65 and older): Older adults may experience more side effects such as diarrhea and low blood cell counts. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver or Kidney Problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as your dose or monitoring plan may need to be adjusted. Children: This medicine has not been studied in patients under 18 years old and is not currently approved for children.
